title: VPAT Vault
summary: Accessibility evidence in, a VPAT 2.5 draft out.
standfirst: A nine-prompt Claude toolkit and local Chrome scanner for turning accessibility evidence into VPAT 2.5 drafts.
stack: Claude prompts · Chrome extension (Manifest V3) · axe-core

plate.alt: Product box for VPAT Vault: a white box with a black spine, a green leaf logo, a large orange 2.1 with an Accessible badge, and the line VPAT, Voluntary Product Accessibility Template, WCAG 2.1 Conformance Report.
plate.caption: The VPAT Vault box: nine prompts, a validator, a dataset, a report template and a Chrome scanner.

paragraphs: I built VPAT Vault to make creating a VPAT simple enough that more websites can publish one. It combines a local Chrome scanner with a prompt toolkit and HTML template, so evidence moves into the report instead of ending up in a separate silo.

sections.heading: Why I made it

image.alt: Illustration: two hands hold a magnifying glass over a bug on a web page covered in accessibility checks.

paragraphs: I wanted a scanning tool I would actually use alongside VPAT creation. The extension captures automated evidence where the work starts, while the prompts and template turn that evidence into a reviewable report. I exercised the workflow with my harness so the pieces stay connected from scan to draft.

The current release includes nine prompts, a dependency-free validator, a 50-record reference dataset, a report template, and a free Manifest V3 Chrome extension that runs axe locally and exports scan evidence. The roadmap is to connect multi-page scan sessions, evidence review, and report generation into one publishable workflow.

sections.heading: Roadmap
sections.intro: A practical path from a working evidence capture tool to a complete VPAT workflow.

roadmap.label: Foundation
roadmap.detail: Nine prompts, validator, 50-record dataset, and HTML report template.

roadmap.label: Local scanner
roadmap.detail: Free Chrome extension runs axe on the active tab and exports canonical scan JSON.

roadmap.label: Scan sessions
roadmap.detail: Capture evidence across multiple pages while keeping findings connected to the report.

roadmap.label: Launch workflow
roadmap.detail: Review evidence, draft rows, run QA, and publish a VPAT from one guided flow.

title: linefield
summary: Twenty generative backgrounds you own outright.
standfirst: Twenty generative line-art backgrounds you own outright.

plate.alt: The top of the linefield gallery: the headline Generative backgrounds, shipped as one file, a short intro, the Wake overlay panel, five collection filters, and the first row of the Currents collection, three monochrome hairline pieces on near-black.
plate.caption: The gallery: twenty pieces in five collections, monochrome by default.

callouts.text: Wake, an opt-in pointer overlay, kept out of the pieces.
Stills by default. The card you point at runs live.

pullQuote: So the checks are scripts now instead of opinions.

paragraphs: A background is the kind of thing you should own outright. It sits on your site for years, it should not phone home, and when you want it slower or bluer you should be able to open the file and change it.

linefield is twenty of them. Each piece is one HTML file with no dependencies and no build step. Tune it with the on-screen controls, hit export, and you get a standalone file with your settings baked in. Paste it into any page and it runs.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: Twenty pieces in five collections, one shared control surface:

items.lead: Monochrome by default.
items.text: Near-white hairlines on near-black, one object per frame, and a declared empty zone where your headline goes. Brightness comes from lines crossing, not from colour. Colour is still one preset away. It just isn't the default any more.

items.lead: Sixteen controls on every piece.
items.text: Scale, speed, stroke, opacity, saturation, color mode, two colors, two hues, invert, glow, angle, motion, phase and density, plus whatever each piece needs on its own. A script drives every control on every piece and diffs the rendered frames: 299 controls, none of them dead. It exists because twice a control shipped that read its value and changed nothing, and both times a human review passed it.

items.lead: Five ways out.
items.text: A baked HTML file with every shared module inlined, the untouched source, PNG at 2x or 4x, SVG, and a written prompt describing the current settings. The baked file is the point. It has zero external references, so it runs from any folder on any host. For decks and mockups there is also a pack of square stills of all twenty, and a catalogue listing each piece's empty zone and controls.

items.lead: Two new materials.
items.text: Dune is a ridge of film grain under one low light. Swell is an ocean swell drawn as a halftone screen, where the size of each dot carries the light. Both step outside pure linework, and both still run in plain Canvas 2D.

items.lead: A gallery that will not cook your laptop.
items.text: Twenty canvas animations running at once will crawl, so the grid shows stills and swaps only the card you are pointing at for a live preview. One at a time, torn down when you look away. Keyboard focus does the same thing, because hover-only interaction is invisible to anyone not using a mouse.

sections.heading: What it actually took
paragraphs: Drawing the pieces was the easy half. The hard half was catching the things that look correct on paper. A control whose maths is right but whose effect is smaller than the line it draws. A baked export that silently produced a blank page for two pieces because a new module was never registered for inlining, which two separate reviews reported as passing.

The worst one was not a bug at all. Five pieces shipped that were each individually fine and collectively looked like one thing, because every review judged a piece against its own intent and never against the others.

So the checks are scripts now instead of opinions. The build refuses to run when the manifest, the pieces and the README disagree. The control audit fails on anything that reads a value without changing a pixel. And the last gate before shipping is looking at all twenty side by side, which is the only one that would have caught the thing a person actually noticed.

sections.heading: Version two
paragraphs: Version one worked and still looked like a demo. Laid out side by side, the problem was colour. Every piece had its own saturated hue, so eighteen pieces read as eighteen different products instead of one collection.

So version two is monochrome first. Every piece was redrawn as one object: hairlines, one bright point, and a lot of empty space for whatever sits on top of it. A new gate fails the build if a default carries colour or marks too much or too little of the frame.
There is no target count. A new piece ships when it clears the same gates as the other twenty.

title: Forma
summary: Pick a shape, set the light, export a transparent PNG.
standfirst: Pick a shape, set the light, export a transparent PNG.
stack: Runs in the browser, no server

plate.alt: Forma editor with a copper torus knot against a dark backdrop and the complete environment picker open, with Midnight selected.
plate.caption: Forma editor. Shape, material and light in one canvas.

callouts.text: Shape, material and light in one canvas.
One search box filters every picker.

paragraphs: A 3D shape on a transparent background is a small ask, and it should not need an account.

Forma is a shape playground that runs in the browser. Pick a shape, give it a material, set the light, and export a transparent PNG. Nothing uploads and nothing needs a server, because the whole thing runs on your machine.

Under the editor is a typed engine that treats shape, material, environment and effect as four separate choices that compose. That is why the same composition can leave as a PNG or as a snippet you paste into a page.

items.lead: Shape, material, environment, effect.
items.text: Eighteen shapes, fifteen materials and six environments, plus effects and presets to start from. Paste an SVG and it extrudes into a shape of its own.

items.lead: Two ways out.
items.text: A transparent PNG, or a self-contained embed snippet with a small browser bundle to sit beside it.

items.lead: Quiet controls.
items.text: Search filters every picker. H hides the panel. Reset puts the default sphere back. On a phone the panel starts collapsed so the shape gets the screen.

items.lead: Free, and yours.
items.text: MIT licensed, no signup, no server. Self-host it or fork it.

sections.heading: What it actually took
paragraphs: The hard part is invisible. Every time you switch a shape or a material, the engine has to hand the old one back to the GPU. Miss one and the tab slowly eats memory. So the test suite cycles compositions at least fifty times across a stratified sample of 360 shape, material and environment combinations, and checks that nothing is left behind.
The render loop is the other quiet piece. One frame scheduler drives everything and pauses when the tab is hidden, so a tab you forgot about is not still rendering.

title: Terry Time
summary: One merch shop, two storefronts, and paid orders pick the winner.
standfirst: A shop for Terry, the face that keeps turning up on East Van walls. I designed seven storefronts, put two of them in a 50/50 split, and wrote down how the winner gets picked before the first visitor arrives.

plate.alt: The two Terry Time storefronts side by side, cobalt blue on warm paper. Left, Store A, the Street Evidence Archive: a three-line headline, a tilted Case 003 stamp and black-and-white street photos filed as evidence. Right, Store B, the Corner Store Receipt: the headline Rung up in East Van beside a long paper receipt that lists a black polo and a black hoodie with dot leaders and prices.
plate.caption: Store A and Store B. A visitor only ever sees one of them.

callouts.text: Store A, the Street Evidence Archive. The shop is a municipal case file: Terry’s photos are filed as evidence and every product is an exhibit.
Store B, the Corner Store Receipt. The catalogue prints as one long thermal receipt from register 07, rung up by Terry.
Same products, prices, size picker and Stripe checkout in both. Nothing is preselected, so the button says *Select a size* until you pick one.

pullQuote: Selling a shirt is easy. Selling one without losing money on it is the job.

paragraphs: Terry is a face that keeps turning up on East Van walls. Terry Time is his shop: a polo, a hoodie and a dad hat, each with the face embroidered on it and made to order.
I designed seven storefronts for it, and every one of them sold the same three things. Picking one on taste would have been a guess, so two of them go live side by side and paid orders decide.
The rule for calling it was written before the first visitor: once each store has had at least 300 visitors, the one with more paid orders per visitor wins. Until then, neither store changes.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: One catalogue, two shops around it:

items.lead: Store A, the Street Evidence Archive.
items.text: The shop as a municipal case file. Terry’s street photos are filed with evidence numbers, and each product is an exhibit with a condition, a marking and a value, stamped *Cleared to wear*.

items.lead: Store B, the Corner Store Receipt.
items.text: The shop as one long thermal receipt: line items, dot leaders, a shelf total and a torn edge. *Thermal paper fades in a week. The list on it stays honest.*

items.lead: One design system under both.
items.text: [Brutal UX](/work/brutal-ux/), ported in cobalt: `#1233c7` ink on warm paper, zero radius, zero shadow. The two shops look nothing alike and share every rule.

image.alt: Exhibit 001 in Store A: a black pique polo on a blue grid, beside a spec table that reads Condition, ready for circulation; Marking, embroidered Terry face; Finish, black; Sizes, S to XL; Value, $37.83 CAD. A Cleared to wear stamp sits in the corner, above a size picker.
image.caption: Exhibit 001 in Store A. The polo, filed like evidence.

items.lead: Seven storefronts is a decision you haven’t made yet.
items.text: A UX audit in September caught it: the home page was a chooser between five shops, so a visitor would land on a design review instead of a store. Five directions went to a branch, and two went into the test.

items.lead: A visitor only ever sees one store.
items.text: Middleware splits `/` and `/shop` 50/50 and pins each visitor to their store with a cookie for 30 days. `?v=a` or `?v=b` forces one, so a post can promise a specific shop, and every Stripe checkout records which store it started in.

items.lead: The rule came before the data.
items.text: Each store needs at least 300 visitors, and the launch promotion has to be over. Then the store with more paid orders per visitor wins. If that’s within noise, the higher average order wins, then the one I’d rather maintain.

items.lead: Honest while it’s off.
items.text: The site builds and runs with no keys at all. Until checkout is switched on, the buttons say it isn’t live yet instead of failing.

sections.heading: After hours
paragraphs: Both stores link to one shoppable lookbook, told in timestamps: 18:51, Dusk, 21:55. Each chapter is a photo, a line and the kit to wear in it, with the size picker right there.

image.alt: The 18:51 chapter of the lookbook: a cobalt-toned photo of a person standing in tall hedges at golden hour, captioned Hedge line, East Van, beside the headline Clock out, a short paragraph and a Kit for 18:51 card with the black polo and its size picker.
image.caption: Hour 01, 18:51. *Clock out.*

sections.heading: What it actually took
paragraphs: The storefronts were the fun part. Selling a shirt is easy. Selling one without losing money on it is the job.

Checkout is Stripe’s hosted page, built from inline prices, so there’s nothing to set up in a dashboard. The browser only sends a product and a quantity. Prices and shipping are always set on the server.

Shipping took the most thought. Stripe’s hosted page can’t re-price by address, so each order pays one shipping line: the higher of Printful’s live Canadian rate and its US rate plus $2. Any address in either country is covered, and a flat rate per country takes over if Printful’s rates are down.

A paid order becomes a Printful draft, not a shipment. The webhook checks the signature, only fulfils sessions that are actually paid, and logs loudly if the order can’t be created, because by then the customer has already paid.

Before real money moves, `npm run verify:live` checks the chain end to end: the API keys, every size linked to a Printful variant, stock, margin per size after Stripe’s fees, a test checkout and the webhook. It also surfaces Printful’s one-time $9.60 embroidery digitization fee, which puts the first order of each design up to $6.40 in the red.

sections.heading: Terry keeps appearing
paragraphs: Footers and error pages draw Terry’s face in a grid of type symbols that never stops switching. It runs on WebGL2, falls back to a canvas still, and holds a single frame for anyone who has asked for reduced motion.

image.alt: The Terry Time 404 page: a boxed message that reads Error 404, Nothing on this wall, beside Terry’s face drawn in hundreds of small blue type symbols.
image.caption: The 404. *This page got painted over, or it never went up. Terry’s still around.*

sections.heading: Roadmap
sections.intro: What’s left between two working storefronts and one winner.

roadmap.label: The build
roadmap.detail: Both stores, the lookbook, sizes, shipping and checkout, with all nine sizes linked to Printful.

roadmap.label: Real-money test
roadmap.detail: Live keys, three real orders landing as Printful drafts, and one shipped to a friend to time the delivery.

roadmap.label: Launch
roadmap.detail: Checkout goes live and the split starts counting.

roadmap.label: Call it
roadmap.detail: At 300 visitors per store, with the launch promotion over, the winner becomes the shop and the other goes to a branch.

title: The Agent Bench
summary: A folder that turns an AI chat tool into an operating environment.
standfirst: Agent Workspace Template and Agentic Light: a folder that turns an AI chat tool into an operating environment, and the same bench with the night shift removed.

status.label: Private, with a public light fork

stack: Codex, Claude Code or the Gemini CLI · plain Markdown

plate.alt: The Agentic Light status dashboard on a dark page: a health banner reading 59 pass, 2 warn, 0 fail, category chips, and the first three preset cards.
plate.caption: Repository health and specialization presets.

callouts.text: The run reports its own health: 59 pass, 2 warn, 0 fail.
Every check is named and counted.
Preset pages are generated from the config files.

paragraphs: Every new AI project started the same way. Copy the agents folder. Copy the skills. Re-add the MCP servers. Re-explain my whole life to a fresh chat window. The work compounded; the setup never did.
The tools get smarter every month. The workspace around them stays dumb. What I wanted was closer to a wood shop than a chat: one bench, tools on the wall, sawdust swept up by someone else overnight.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: One folder holds the agents, tools and routines I use across projects:

items.lead: An orchestrator and seven scoped agents.
items.text: The root agent breaks work down and hands it to a specialist: architect, coder, engineering manager, archivist, curator, plus a creative director for brand and copy and a QA agent that gatekeeps production pull requests. The five core roles ship for all three CLIs; QA runs on Codex and Claude, creative direction on Claude only. Each one owns its lane and nothing else.

items.lead: Vault Brain, a second brain in plain Markdown.
items.text: Clip a web page in your browser and a background job reads it overnight, files it into a wiki, and cross-links it to everything you already know. Raw notes get the same treatment. Nothing evaporates in chat history.

items.lead: Background jobs that keep it honest.
items.text: Daily ingest, a Friday close-out that summarizes the week, a Monday job that starts the next one, a health check every four hours, and an hourly sync that keeps new skills stocked on the shelf. When something breaks, the system says so before you notice.

sections.outro: The template runs on Codex, Claude Code, or the Gemini CLI, and picks up the GitHub CLI and Playwright when they are installed, so the agents push code and test pages as shell commands instead of burning tokens on plumbing. Built for the Mac first; the agents and the vault run anywhere the CLI does. If you want the same bench without the night shift, that is Agentic Light.

items.lead: One owner per layer.
items.text: Delivery owns the projects, automation owns the schedule, knowledge owns the vault. Nothing falls between the cracks because every crack has a name on it.

items.lead: Boring formats win.
items.text: The vault is plain Markdown and the files are the store. If I walk away from every tool in this stack tomorrow, the knowledge walks with me.

items.lead: The system reports its own health.
items.text: Trust in automation is a UX problem, and visibility is the fix. A status page tells me which job failed while I slept and what to do about it, and the docs ship with a failure-mode playbook: what breaks, why, and the exact prompt to hand a model to fix it.

sections.heading: The light fork: Agentic Light
paragraphs: The Agent Workspace Template runs all night. Daily ingest, a Friday close-out, a health check every four hours. That is the right shape when you live in it. It is the wrong shape when you want to point an agent at one repo for an afternoon.

Agentic Light is the same bench with the night shift removed. No scheduler, no background service, no retry queue. You start it by hand, one provider runs once in the foreground, and you watch what it does.

sections.heading: What the light fork is
sections.intro: A small fork you specialize once, then run by hand:

items.lead: Six roles, cut down to what you need.
items.text: It ships as a generic fork with architect, coder, engineering manager, curator, creative director and QA. Run one script and it becomes a specific tool: you pick the roles, the gates, and the skills the router may reach for.

items.lead: Six presets to start from.
items.text: A web app, a CLI tool, a data pipeline, a design review, a server review and a WCAG audit. Each preset decides which roles switch on, which gates run before a pull request opens, and which skills are on the shelf. The WCAG preset runs Playwright, axe and a VPAT lint.

items.lead: Four providers, one run.
items.text: Claude, Gemini, Codex or Ollama, in the order you set. If the first choice is missing, the launcher falls back before anything starts. Once a run starts it is never retried, and Ollama will not run a workflow that writes. A fake-binary test suite covers all of it without touching a real provider.

items.lead: A second brain that knows the project.
items.text: Plain Markdown records with offline full-text search and optional Ollama embeddings. When you ask for it, a context packet gets prepended to the coder's prompt. The index is disposable and rebuilds from the files, so the Markdown stays the store.

items.lead: A dashboard that reads its own config.
items.text: A static microsite shows repo health, every preset, and which roles each one switches on. The preset and roster pages are generated from the config files, and it opens straight from a folder, with no server and no build.

sections.heading: The UX thinking, without a night shift

items.lead: Nothing runs that you did not start.
items.text: Every background job is a place for something to fail while you are not looking. Removing the scheduler removes that whole class of surprise.

items.lead: Specialize once, commit the result.
items.text: Specializing writes three config files: the active roles, the gate list and the selected skills. In a fork you commit them, so the setup lives in the repo, not in anyone's memory.

items.lead: One human gate, and it does not auto-approve.
items.text: The gates you picked run first. Then the run stops and waits for a yes at the terminal. Only after that can anything open a pull request.

paragraphs: The future of a workspace is not a grand digital mansion you maintain forever. It is a bench that sharpens its own tools and remembers everything you put down on it. The repository is private; this case study shows how I use it.

title: UX Skill Repo 1.0
summary: Twelve agent skills held to one measurable rulebook.
standfirst: Twelve AI agent skills held to one measurable rulebook, with a loop that keeps testing it against real work.
stack: Agent skills for Claude Code and Cursor

paragraphs: Ask a general AI to review your interface and you get a pep talk: make it feel simpler, tighten the hierarchy, smooth out the flow. It sounds like feedback. It changes nothing, because the model has no floor to hold itself to and no way to prove its advice actually works.

UX Skill Repo is the fix: twelve narrowly scoped AI agent skills, strategists, critics, writers, builders, run by one orchestrator and held to a single measurable standard instead of general-purpose opinion.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: One repo, twelve skills, one shared rulebook.

items.lead: A shared vocabulary, not twelve opinions.
items.text: Craft rules live once in design-rules.md, cited by ID (R-COL-1, R-BAN-6). UX heuristics live in ux_laws.json, cited by name. No skill restates “use 4.5:1 contrast” in its own words and drifts out of sync.

items.lead: Skills grouped by job, not origin.
items.text: Plan (ux-governance, ux-strategy), review (ui-expert, ux-black-hat), make (front-end-design, implement-design, canvas-design, brand-steward, ux-writer), and meta (orchestrator, improvement-loop, find-skills) all route through one front door.

items.lead: A loop that finds its own bugs.
items.text: improvement-loop runs audit, execute, systematize, re-audit, escalate, and won’t advance a round unless the rulebook itself learned something. Six rounds in, it’s caught its own accent color failing contrast as text, a selection state that broke in dark mode, and a fully built page nothing on the site linked to.

sections.outro: I run the skills from .agents/skills/ in Claude Code and Cursor. The repository is private; this case study covers the rules and review loop.

items.lead: Feedback that can’t cite a number isn’t feedback.
items.text: Every finding ties to a contrast ratio or a named law, so “improve the hierarchy” becomes a rule ID and a fix, not a vibe.

items.lead: The rulebook only grows from evidence.
items.text: It started at nine color rules and six interaction rules. It’s grown because rounds kept finding real, unstaged bugs, not because someone guessed a rule might matter someday.

items.lead: A clean pass that teaches nothing doesn’t count.
items.text: Advancing a round requires two things: no blocking findings left, and the rulebook learned something new. That forces harder test surfaces, like a data-dense ops console built specifically because a static landing page had run out of complexity to break.

paragraphs: The easy version of this story stops at “I hardened my own landing page.” The harder one is proving the loop generalizes to something built without the answer already in mind, which is what that harder surface is for.

title: Brutal UX
summary: Every soft-UI cue removed at once, and the trade defended in writing.
standfirst: A design system that removes every soft-UI hierarchy cue at once, and defends the trade in writing.

paragraphs: Most redesigns dial decoration down a little: a smaller shadow, a tighter radius, one fewer gradient. Brutal UX asks a blunter question: what's actually load-bearing if you remove all of it at once? No rounded corners. No shadows. No gradients. No easing. No custom font.
The bet is that hierarchy doesn't disappear when you strip the decoration. It just moves, from the channel your eye scans automatically to the one you have to read.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: One enforcement layer, applied globally and irreversibly:

items.lead: Every soft-UI cue removed at once, not dialed down.
items.text: Zero border-radius, zero box-shadow, zero transition duration, system monospace only, all forced with `!important` at the root so no component can quietly opt back in.

items.lead: Hierarchy still exists, it just moved.
items.text: A five-step type scale (48/32/24/16/13px) and 2-3px black borders carry the entire structure that shadow and rounding used to carry.

items.lead: Color is rationed like a budget, not a palette.
items.text: Red for alerts, green for live data, blue for raw hyperlinks, never decoration, never the only signal a state changed.

items.lead: Removing polish doesn't remove hierarchy, it relocates it.
items.text: From the pre-attentive visual channel to the semantic one. The system's own validation pass names the trade directly: novices pay a visual-search penalty, experts get near-zero-friction spatial memory.

items.lead: Instant feedback is a decision, not a missing feature.
items.text: Every transition and animation duration is zeroed globally. State changes land in the same frame instead of easing into existence, an anvil dropping, not a soft landing.

items.lead: A brutal system still has to pass accessibility, or it's just ugly.
items.text: The manifesto ships its own amendments: a loud, instant focus ring, uppercase capped at short labels only, and color always paired with text so it's never the sole carrier of meaning.

paragraphs: Most design systems soften over time. This one is the control group. Building the extreme version first makes it obvious which comfort you're actually buying when you add rounding, shadow, or motion back in.
[Terry Time](/work/terry-time/) is built on it, in cobalt.

title: Classic Cottrell Design System
summary: Tokens, primitives and a showcase that documents itself.
standfirst: A token-driven, multi-theme design system pairing a warm editorial canvas with reusable React primitives.
stack: CSS custom properties · React 19 · Base UI

paragraphs: Every new interface started as a fresh set of decisions: which green, which radius, which type pairing, made again from scratch each time and drifting a little further from the last one. Re-theming meant hunting down hardcoded values across a dozen components.

The Classic Cottrell Design System is the fix: one set of CSS custom properties for color, type, and spacing, and a library of primitives built on top of them, so re-theming is a values-only edit instead of a rewrite.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: One token layer, one component library, one showcase that proves both:

items.lead: A warm, editorial baseline.
items.text: A cream canvas, a single forest-green accent, and a Rosarivo-serif / Red Hat Display-sans pairing, defined once as CSS variables in globals.css and mapped to light and dark themes.

items.lead: Primitives, not one-off pages.
items.text: Button, Card, Input, Badge, and the rest live in components/ui/, built with React 19 and Base UI primitives, so every demo page — landing, form, about, gallery — assembles entirely from the same reusable set.

items.lead: The showcase is the documentation.
items.text: The home page renders the tokens, type, and components live, so what you see is what you get, not a static style guide that drifts out of sync with the code.

title: ClassicCottrell CLI
summary: A CLI framework so every new tool starts branded, not blank.
standfirst: A reusable CLI framework so every new tool starts branded, not blank.

plate.alt: Product box for the Photo Curation Skill v1: a white box with a black spine, a green aperture logo, a large orange v1 with an AI-powered badge, and the line Photo Curation Skill, Provider-Neutral Real Estate Photo Selection.
plate.caption: Photo Curator CLI, the first shipped product on the framework.

paragraphs: Every new internal tool started the same way: a blank argparse script, a copy-pasted color function, a welcome message written once and never touched again. The branding lived in whichever script wrote it last.
ClassicCottrell CLI is the fix: subclass a Brand, register a few commands, and every tool that ships gets the same welcome page, the same terminal styling, and the same fallback behavior for free.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.intro: One framework, three fields to brand it:

items.lead: Brand once, in three fields.
items.text: Subclass Brand with a name, tagline, and hex accent, and every command inherits a welcome page, an ASCII-rendered logo, and a branded first-run splash. No copy-paste between projects.

items.lead: Terminal color that actually degrades.
items.text: The success/warning/error/info helpers detect truecolor, 256-color, or 16-color terminals automatically, fall back to plain text under NO_COLOR or a pipe, and never assume a capability that isn't there.

items.lead: Three bundled apps prove the framework holds up.
items.text: ccasset (responsive image variants and blurhash), ccsync (frontmatter validation and content indexing), and cctokens (CSS custom-property extraction) each ship in roughly 80 to 145 lines because the framework does the heavy lifting, not the app.

items.lead: A first run should look considered, not empty.
items.text: Every tool built on the framework gets the same branded welcome page and splash banner by default, so “we didn’t have time for onboarding” stops being the default outcome.

items.lead: Degrade honestly instead of assuming a terminal.
items.text: Color support is detected, not assumed, so the same command reads correctly whether it's a modern terminal, an old one, or a log file redirected to disk.

items.lead: White-labeling should never require a fork.
items.text: Every brand token overrides through an env var prefix at runtime, so the same framework ships five differently branded tools without five copies of the code.

sections.heading: Photo Curator CLI: a real product on the framework
sections.intro: The framework needed proof it could carry a shipped product, not just internal tools. Photo Curator CLI is that proof:

items.lead: Automated shortlisting, not manual triage.
items.text: Point it at a shoot folder and it scores every frame, then ranks a keep/reject shortlist automatically — the first pass done for you, fast, instead of scrubbing hundreds of near-duplicates by eye.

items.lead: Thresholds you set, not a black box.
items.text: Keep/reject cutoffs are configurable, so the tool's judgment stays tunable to how strict a pass you actually want.

items.lead: Built on the same branded shell as everything else.
items.text: It ships as a command-line tool on the Classic Cottrell CLI toolkit, so it inherits the same welcome page, terminal styling, and fallback behavior as ccasset, ccsync, and cctokens for free.

paragraphs: The measure of a framework isn't the first tool built on it, it's the fifth. Three internal apps and one shipped product in, the pattern's held: brand a class, register a command, ship.

title: Creative services
summary: Six years of campaigns for adidas, the NBA, MLS and E.D. Smith, and the platform behind them.
standfirst: From 2011 to 2017 I designed cross-channel campaigns at Tagga: for adidas with the NBA, the NCAA and MLS, for E.D. Smith, and for brands like Kicking Horse Coffee and Lindt. Then I led the UI of the customer data platform they all fed.
stack: Campaign sites · Social · In-store print · SMS

paragraphs: Tagga was a small team running cross-channel campaigns for national and international brands. Past adidas and E.D. Smith, the list ran from Kicking Horse Coffee, Lindt and Sun-Maid to Gordmans, Vita Foods and Banamex.

Under the creative, every campaign had the same job: turn someone in a store, a stadium or a feed into a profile the brand could use. In my last two years I moved onto the platform that did that, as its UI/UX lead.

items.lead: adidas: engaged fans.
items.text: adidas wanted to find the people who bought team gear and talked about it, and group them with their teams, online and off. Retailers and teams promoted photo and video contests on their own social channels, with VIP experiences, weekly ticket giveaways and signed merchandise as prizes.

items.lead: #NBASwingman.
items.text: To find the real market for the swingman jersey, fans filmed *How Swingman are you?* videos and posted them on Instagram or Vine with the campaign hashtag. The prize was two tickets to the NBA Finals.

items.lead: NCAA football and basketball.
items.text: Event campaigns. I designed for jumbotrons and stadium video boards that asked fans to text a keyword to a short code. The reply was a link to a mobile entry page.

items.lead: MLS.
items.text: To help MLS compete with the bigger U.S. leagues, adidas wanted to know who its fans were. Over two seasons we ran in-store signings and displays, social posts and photo-contest sites for VIP game experiences.

items.lead: E.D. Smith: TasteCreator.
items.text: The 133-year-old Canadian brand had an out-of-date website and no social presence. Over three years we built TasteCreator, an online community that became the new face of the brand, with new social channels, a new website and 14 seasonal campaigns aimed at a younger audience.

image.alt: Three MLS posters for stores, side by side, for Sporting Kansas City, Seattle Sounders FC and the Philadelphia Union. Each shows a player above the line Win a VIP game experience, a QR code, a keyword to text to 82442, and the prizes: weekly ticket giveaways and a grand prize of game tickets, a gift card, pre-game field access and a post-game meet and greet.
image.caption: In store for MLS: a stanchion card, a four-way banner and an H-frame panel, each with its own keyword and QR code.

sections.heading: How a campaign worked
paragraphs: Every campaign ran on one flow. Each channel had its own URL, keyword or hashtag, from a store stand or a stadium screen to a tweet or an email banner. They all led to one responsive landing page and one entry form, often with social sign-in to make entering easier.
Entering always paid something back: exclusive content, a coupon or a store locator. Then the platform mapped and grouped the people behind the entries into profiles the brand could use.
We also made the content calendars and collateral that teams, players and retailers used to keep each campaign going.

image.alt: A wireframe flow. Online channels (social media, desktop, web and email banners, Google) and in-store channels (in-store stands and in-stadium screens, with SMS and QR codes) all point to one responsive landing page with an entry form. It leads to a thank-you page with a coupon code, then to a store locator and a social takeover page, with Facebook and Twitter share links looping back to the form.
image.caption: The campaign flow: every channel, online or in store, led to one entry form, then a coupon, a store locator or exclusive content.

sections.heading: The platform
paragraphs: All those entries fed Tagga’s own software. When I started it was a white-label SMS and mobile-site platform. It grew into a cross-channel campaign reporting tool, then a customer data platform that turned raw data from campaigns, APIs, file uploads and point-of-sale systems into customer profiles.

As UI/UX lead I worked with the product designer and the CTO. I started on paper, sketching layouts and motion from the user stories, and took the sketches to the front-end developer before the whole team reviewed them. When we disagreed on a flow, I built each version, sometimes as a video, so everyone could see it work before we chose. The last step was a working prototype in Adobe XD for the front-end developer.

image.alt: Pencil sketches of interface layouts and a flow diagram on sheets of paper, on a desk in front of a laptop, with a purple ruler, markers and pencils.
image.caption: Paper first, before anything went on screen.

sections.heading: The segment page
paragraphs: The segment page holds the groups of customers a brand cares about, like people who abandon their carts. It had to bend with the roadmap as the company grew and clients asked for more.

My first version was one long list. That broke when bigger clients had hundreds of segments. I tried two fixes: the page split between the list and segment groups, and folders in a sidebar the client could sort segments into. The sidebar won.

Later the detail panel’s tabs were hard to read, and information disappeared as you switched between them. I replaced the tabs with an accordion and kept a summary at the top that stays put, whichever section is open.

image.alt: Two versions of the My Segments page. The first is a single list of three segments with profile counts and who created them. The final one adds a sidebar of segment folders on the left and a Segment Info panel on the right with the profile count, export and edit buttons, and collapsible sections for rules, snapshots and exports.
image.caption: The segment page, first and final: one long list, then folders in a sidebar and a summary panel.

sections.heading: What it actually took
paragraphs: A small team doing everything. On most campaigns I was lead designer, front-end developer, UX and QA at once: the key visuals, the in-store print, the social posts, the responsive entry site, and the testing before it went live.

Over three years of E.D. Smith campaigns the team went from five people to two, which put the client relationship and the creative in my hands. For the Triple Fruits back-to-school campaign I worked with the recipe photography team on the key photo, directing how the items were laid out.
Before Tagga I spent ten years in print, making signs and running large-format printers and presses.
